\begin{table*}[!tp]\centering\small
\caption{The configuration guide. Each row pairs a grading scenario with a recommended setting and the trade-off behind it.}\label{tab:framework}
\begin{tabular}{p{2.8cm}p{4.2cm}p{9.2cm}}
\hline
Scenario & Recommended & Trade-off in the rule \\
\hline
\raggedright Choosing the model & \raggedright The strongest model that does not collapse to zero, with reasoning off (here GLM-5.1, for both tasks) & On the five datasets it stayed 0.000 to 0.077 QWK below the best configuration in hindsight, at up to 30 times lower cost; the cheapest model gave up 0.073 to 0.131 for a further cost saving (Table~\ref{tab:guideregret}) \\[3pt]
\hline
\raggedright Grading short answers & \raggedright Reasoning off & The reasoning gain is small and none survives correction for multiple comparisons (before correction it is significant only for Qwen on Mohler and SemEval), while reasoning on uses 9--925 times the output tokens \\[3pt]
\hline
\raggedright Grading code, the baseline collapses to zero & \raggedright Reasoning on, or switch to a discriminating model & Reasoning recovers the discrimination the collapsed baseline lost (Qwen $+0.113$ QWK on PT-CS code), but at 714 to 844 times the output tokens and worse run-to-run consistency, so switching model is often the better fix \\[3pt]
\hline
\raggedright Grading code, the baseline does not collapse & \raggedright Reasoning off; on only if local validation justifies it & Without the collapse the reasoning gain is inconsistent and not predictable in advance, so off is the safe default, saving cost (about 109--211$\times$ the tokens) and keeping consistency \\[3pt]
\hline
\raggedright Consistency or fairness is critical & \raggedright Reasoning off & Reasoning on is less reproducible, partly a length effect and partly reasoning itself \\[3pt]
\hline
\raggedright A rubric or reference answer is available & \raggedright Supply it as guidance (rubric for code, reference answer for short answers) & Guidance was the one change that reliably raised agreement: it helped in 11 of 12 model-dataset combinations across three model families ($+0.095$ to $+0.256$ QWK), at the cost of only the extra prompt tokens \\[3pt]
\hline
\raggedright The rubric has several criteria & \raggedright Holistic scoring (one overall score) & Across two models and two code datasets, scoring criterion by criterion never improved agreement ($-0.072$ to $+0.029$ QWK, worse in one case) at about 2 times the cost per answer \\[3pt]
\hline
\raggedright The exam has several questions & \raggedright Grade one question per call & On PT-CS code, grading the whole exam in one call never improved agreement (Qwen $-0.091$ QWK, significant; DeepSeek $-0.024$) and even cost 7\% more per question \\[3pt]
\hline
\raggedright Grading many answers in sequence & \raggedright Fresh conversation per question; no history carried across the exam & A shared, accumulating conversation lowered grades slightly (0.010 to 0.027 of the scale) and answer order moved individual grades by about 0.09 (three models, up to 80 exams) \\[3pt]
\hline
\end{tabular}
